old: The tariff side of the same trade environment is the counterweight. BoatPro’s tariff brief, drawn from The Washington Post and Forbes, documents the 5 April 2025 executive order under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act which raised effective US tariff rates on imported yachts: China 20 to 40 percent, Turkey 10 to 25, Taiwan 10 to 20, Italy 2.2 to 15, Germany 1.4 to 15, France 1.2 to 15, Netherlands 0.7 to 15, UK 0.97 to 10. In May 2025 the US Court of International Trade ruled the President did not have authority to impose these tariffs under IEEPA, a ruling upheld on appeal and, after argument in November 2025, by the Supreme Court; by spring 2026 the trade court had ordered nationwide refunds. For a US-based first-time new-build buyer, the headline price from a Northern European yard now carries roughly fifteen percentage points of tariff exposure that was not in the contract eighteen months earlier; some buyers are responding by acquiring duty-paid hulls from US dealer inventory rather than ordering direct.
new: The tariff side of the same trade environment has changed three times since April 2025. BoatPro’s tariff brief, drawn from The Washington Post and Forbes, documents the April 2025 tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), which raised effective US tariff rates on imported yachts: China 20 to 40 percent, Turkey 10 to 25, Taiwan 10 to 20, Italy 2.2 to 15, Germany 1.4 to 15, France 1.2 to 15, Netherlands 0.7 to 15, UK 0.97 to 10. On 20 February 2026 the Supreme Court held that IEEPA does not authorise tariffs, and on 4 March the Court of International Trade ordered the duties refunded to all importers of record. A temporary 10 percent tariff under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 applied from 24 February to 24 July 2026. Since 24 July most imports have carried Section 301 duties of 10 or 12.5 percent, with a ceiling on the combined duty for goods from the European Union. A US buyer ordering from a European yard should confirm the rate that applies at contract and delivery, and the contract should say who bears any change. In 2025 some buyers responded by acquiring duty-paid hulls from US dealer inventory rather than ordering direct.
